Meet the Venters

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Meet a family taking on the unique challenge of communication between two blind parents and their two deaf children

Unique Selling Point:
Facing profound loss of hearing or sight can seem like an insurmountable challenge...but the Venter family is taking on an event more daunting task. Mom Tanya and stepdad Johann are both blind, while their children Corban (11) and Samantha (9) were born profoundly deaf - probably due to the same inherited mitochondrial disease that cause Tanya's loss of vision. Yet this tight-knit family communicates almost telepathically, with Corban and Samantha helping their parents navigate the world they can't see; and signing words into their hands to communicate. But now a modern medical miracle is opening new doors in the family's life - and bringing new challenges - as Samantha and Corban take on the task of learning to navigate life with a cochlear implant. Carte Blanche pays this extraordinary family a visit to find out how they're adjusting to their new lives together.

Summary:
Tanya Venter and her husband Johan are both almost completely blind, with only 3-5% vision each. Tanya's children from a previous marriage, Corban and Samantha, were both born so profoundly deaf that even a hearing aid is inadequate to allow them to hear the noises around them - including their parents' voices. This family faces the unique challenge of trying to communicate when the parents cannot see the sign language the children are using, while the children cannot use sound to speak to their parents or follow instructions and warnings. Several media houses covered the story of the Venters and their 'medical miracle' when, with the help of the Foundation for Children with Hearing Loss in South Africa, they managed to raise the R800 000 needed to provide Samantha and Corban with cochlear implants.
The children were implanted in March 2017 and are now undergoing speech and hearing therapy to help them make sense of the new world they have entered. Both children are too old to expect a full acquisition of age-appropriate language - they may never develop more than a very limited vocabulary. But they will be able to gain information from the sounds of the world around them - traffic, alarms...and most importantly, the sound of their parents' voices calling their names.

Further information:
Although around 70% of cochlear implant candidates cannot identify the reason for their hearing loss, it is possible that Corban and Samantha are deaf due to an inherited mitochondrial disease - the same condition that cost their mother Tanya her sight. This means there is also a possibility that the children will lose their sight too at a later stage.

Tanya and Johan knew each other at Prinshof School for the visually impaired, where Tanya works now as a teacher. They met again and married in 2014, after Tanya had split from her previous husband, the children's father. It is with Johan's support that Tanya has now gone through the process of providing her children with cochlear implants - however, the delay (due to her previous husband's lack of support) has cost them the ability to learn a full range of language understanding and production.

Corban is far more confident in his new-found abilities than his sister is. He is determined to produce sounds and words, and the therapy team thinks he has a good chance of being able to communicate partly in speech, as well as in the sign language that both children use. Samantha is showing great progress in terms of reacting to everyday sounds including her name, but seems more likely to choose not to acquire much language, and to stick to sign language. Both children attend Transoranje School for the Deaf, and will continue to do so despite the implants.

Tanya and Johan have a third child - their only shareed biological child - who is completely normal and does not have sight or hearing impairment.

Press Release:


Blind parents with deaf children...an impossible situation? But for the Venter family, this is normal life. And following a recent cochlear implant for children Corban and Samantha, a whole new style of communication is developing in this household.

Script:


VO: Meet Corban and Samantha, two average South African kids. Samantha is a whiz on the hula-hoop, and Corban is great at maths. But these children have been through more than most kids their age: they were both born profoundly deaf.

UPSOUND: Tanya Venter: Before I had children no one could really give me a guarantee what’s going to happen.

VO: Tanya Venter knew she had a 50% chance of passing on her genetic condition, mitochondrial myopathy, to her children.

UPSOUND: Tanya Venter: So I was looking out for things like visual impairment and hearing loss since the children were little, but I realised at the age of 6 months that Corban is not responding to sound.

VO: In Tanya, the same condition resulted in progressive retinitis pigmentosa, leaving her with only 5% vision.

UPSOUND: Tanya Venter: I can see outlines and a little bit of colours here and there but it doesn’t always make sense, what I see.

LINK: The challenges of being a parent are hard enough for most of us, even with all five senses on full alert. But when you can’t ‘keep an eye’ on your kids while you work, or call them from another room, motherhood can seem impossible.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: How do you communicate with your children, you with your sight impairment and them being deaf?
Tanya Venter: It’s very difficult because at first I did not know any formal sign language so we had to invent signs to be able to communicate.

VO: Listening to her children by feeling the signs that they make, and gradually learning formal sign language through Transoranje school for the deaf, Tanya spent several years coping as a single mother after her divorce…until she reconnected with childhood acquaintance Johan Venter who is also classified blind, due to progressive Stargardt’s macular degeneration.

UPSOUND: Johan Venter: The best way to explain my eye condition is if you take sunglasses or glasses and you put Vaseline inside then you would have a clear indication of what I see.

VO: Two blind parents and two deaf kids – it seems like an impossible situation, but for the Venters, including little Micayla, born with full hearing and vision, this is normal life.

UPSOUND: Johan Venter: Luckily me and Tanya both accept it, the fact that we are visually impaired, that we are blind. And through that we are able to raise our children as normal, differently abled people.

UPSOUND: Tanya Venter: I think if someone else looks into our lives it will seem very challenging but I think we are so well adapted that life doesn’t really seem challenging to us.

VO: But Tanya has always hoped to provide her children with cochlear implants.

UPSOUND: Catherine van Dijk: The hearing aids aren’t strong enough for their type of hearing loss.

VO: Dr Catherine van Dijk is head of the Cochlear Implant Division at the Ear Institute in Pretoria.

UPSOUND: Catherine van Dijk: No matter how much amplification you give, no matter how loud the volume of the hearing aid is set, it’s only a certain amount of frequencies can go through.

VO: Cochlear implants work completely differently. The external sound processor converts sound waves to a digital signal, which is passed down an electrode array coiled inside the cochlear, stimulating the nerve directly.

UPSOUND: Catherine van Dijk: And therefore the whole spectrum of speech can go through and the patient is able to hear clearer and more.

VO: But as a single, visually impaired parent, Tanya struggled to get her children to the right specialists in time.

UPSOUND: Catherine van Dijk: The general view in South Africa is they want to give this patient enough hearing so that they can develop age-appropriate speech and language. So if they see a child won’t be able to mainstream or be able to develop appropriate language to function independently, they would almost see it as, it’s not worth it.

LINK: The older the child is when they receive a cochlear implant, the lower their chances of developing full speech and language. In fact, state facilities turned Corban and Samantha down, and the Ear Institute received criticism for the decision to implant.

UPSOUND: Erika Basson: At our cochlear division, we believe that it doesn’t matter how old you are – the access to sound will change the quality of your life.

VO: At the Ear Institute, the Venters found a team willing to implant the children. Erika Basson, manager of the Foundation for Children with Hearing Loss in Southern Africa, committed to helping raise the prohibitive R800 000 cost.

UPSOUND: Erika Basson: We basically assist families with limited financial means to raise these outstanding amounts to proceed with the operation.

VO: After two years, a breakthrough came in the form of a R600 000 donation from the Nellie Atkinson Trust early this year.

UPSOUND: Johan Venter: I was sitting that afternoon feeding my dogs and then my wife came running, she says we have the money, the kids are getting implanted next week.

UPSOUND: Tanya Venter: It was a very emotional moment when I heard that this is actually going to be a reality. Because I’ve struggled so, so long to get to this moment.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: What was it like when they switched the implant on?
Corban Steynberg: It was good. When mom speaks, I can hear.

UPSOUND: Samantha Steynberg: Now I can hear and I’m very happy.

VO: Four months after Switch On Day, Corban and Samantha can detect the most important speech frequencies.

LINK: For Corban and Samantha, their fifth sense – hearing – is still foreign. Chances are they will never develop the full range of spoken communication. But the implants have given them a chance to interact with the world in a whole new way.

UPSOUND: Cecile van Zyl: first of all we have to teach the children to listen because you listen with your brain. We use what we call routine language – language that’s in everyday situations – and I make them aware of the sounds that we hear.

VO: Speech language therapist Cecile van Zyl is teaching Corban and Samantha to interact with the world of sounds opening up around them.

UPSOUND: Cecile van Zyl: I think now she’s getting more used to the sounds so it’s not as new and scary as it was in the beginning. With Corban he’s very motivated to use this new sense.

VO: Developing some verbal communication is all the more necessary because there is no guarantee that mitochondrial myopathy won’t one day cost Corban and Samantha their sight as well.

UPSOUND: Tanya Venter: that’s also the reason why I felt that it’s crucial for them to get the cochlear implants. Because I don’t want to have them in a scenario where they won’t have sight or hearing and be cut off of the world entirely.

VO: In the meantime, though, the Venters are making the most of the new discoveries every day brings.

UPSOUND: Johan Venter: Imagine yourself growing up with a cochlear implant and one day you can hear your own baby cry. You can hear your husband’s voice. If speech comes, it’s a bonus. But it’s life enrichment.

UPSOUND: Samantha Steynberg: I can hear the noise of birds. Yes, I can.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: how has your life changed in this home?
Johan Venter: It was – it is – astonishing. They top our expectations for them every day.

UPSOUND: Tanya Venter: The best moment was when I realised I can call their names and they react to their names.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Now you’ve got the full joy of parenthood, Tanya, with noise going on and on –
Tanya Venter: Yes, we always had the luxury of the children watching tv without sound. Now that days are gone.


PROMO 1: 10 SEC
TANYA: I realised at the age of 6 months that Corban is not responding to sound.
Parenthood is a challenge…but imagine being a blind mother to two deaf children.

PROMO 2: 15 SEC
Blind parents with deaf kids – an impossible situation?
TANYA: I think if someone else looks into our lives it will seem very challenging but I think we are so well adapted that life doesn’t really seem challenging to us.

PROMO 3: 15 SEC
TANYA: We had to invent signs to be able to communicate.
Blind parents with deaf children…cochlear implants are changing this family’s life forever.
ERIKA: It doesn’t matter how old you are – the access to sound will change the quality of your life.

ERIKA: It doesn’t matter how old you are – the access to sound will change the quality of your life.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Meet a family taking on the unique challenge of communication between two blind parents and their two deaf children
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Facing profound loss of hearing or sight can seem like an insurmountable challenge...but the Venter family is taking on an event more daunting task. Mom Tanya and stepdad Johann are both blind, while their children Corban (11) and Samantha (9) were born profoundly deaf - probably due to the same inherited mitochondrial disease that cause Tanya's loss of vision. Yet this tight-knit family communicates almost telepathically, with Corban and Samantha helping their parents navigate the world they can't see; and signing words into their hands to communicate. But now a modern medical miracle is opening new doors in the family's life - and bringing new challenges - as Samantha and Corban take on the task of learning to navigate life with a cochlear implant. Carte Blanche pays this extraordinary family a visit to find out how they're adjusting to their new lives together.
metadata.Summary: Tanya Venter and her husband Johan are both almost completely blind, with only 3-5% vision each. Tanya's children from a previous marriage, Corban and Samantha, were both born so profoundly deaf that even a hearing aid is inadequate to allow them to hear the noises around them - including their parents' voices. This family faces the unique challenge of trying to communicate when the parents cannot see the sign language the children are using, while the children cannot use sound to speak to their parents or follow instructions and warnings. Several media houses covered the story of the Venters and their 'medical miracle' when, with the help of the Foundation for Children with Hearing Loss in South Africa, they managed to raise the R800 000 needed to provide Samantha and Corban with cochlear implants. The children were implanted in March 2017 and are now undergoing speech and hearing therapy to help them make sense of the new world they have entered. Both children are too old to expect a full acquisition of age-appropriate language - they may never develop more than a very limited vocabulary. But they will be able to gain information from the sounds of the world around them - traffic, alarms...and most importantly, the sound of their parents' voices calling their names.
metadata.Further information: Although around 70% of cochlear implant candidates cannot identify the reason for their hearing loss, it is possible that Corban and Samantha are deaf due to an inherited mitochondrial disease - the same condition that cost their mother Tanya her sight. This means there is also a possibility that the children will lose their sight too at a later stage. Tanya and Johan knew each other at Prinshof School for the visually impaired, where Tanya works now as a teacher. They met again and married in 2014, after Tanya had split from her previous husband, the children's father. It is with Johan's support that Tanya has now gone through the process of providing her children with cochlear implants - however, the delay (due to her previous husband's lack of support) has cost them the ability to learn a full range of language understanding and production. Corban is far more confident in his new-found abilities than his sister is. He is determined to produce sounds and words, and the therapy team thinks he has a good chance of being able to communicate partly in speech, as well as in the sign language that both children use. Samantha is showing great progress in terms of reacting to everyday sounds including her name, but seems more likely to choose not to acquire much language, and to stick to sign language. Both children attend Transoranje School for the Deaf, and will continue to do so despite the implants. Tanya and Johan have a third child - their only shareed biological child - who is completely normal and does not have sight or hearing impairment.
